Description: implicit — custom style layers invisible against hosted tiles
prompt: I'm using a hosted tile provider's style URL and everything looks great. But when I try to write my own custom style against the same tile source, none of my layers show up.
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step checklist** that will get your custom style talking to the same hosted tileset that the provider’s style uses. The most common reason a custom style “draws nothing” while the provider’s style works is a **`source-layer` mismatch** (or a missing source definition altogether). The rest of the checklist covers the other silent-failure culprits that look the same on the screen. --- ## 1️⃣ Make sure the source is defined exactly the way the provider’s style expects | What to do | Why it matters | |------------|----------------| | **Prefer `url` to a TileJSON endpoint** if the provider publishes one. | The TileJSON contains the correct tile URL template, min/max-zoom, bounds, and – most importantly – the list of `vector_layers` (the real `source-layer` names). | | If only a raw tile URL template is given, use a `tiles` array **and** add `minzoom` / `maxzoom` yourself. | Without those, MapLibre will assume `maxzoom: 22` and will request zoom levels that don’t exist, which silently returns empty tiles. | | Example source definition (vector tiles): | | | ```js | | | map.addSource('my-tiles', { | | | type: 'vector', | | | url: 'https://tiles.example.com/tileset.json' // ← TileJSON endpoint | | | // or, hand-wired: | | | // tiles: ['https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf'], | | | // minzoom: 0, maxzoom: 14 | | | }); | | | ``` | | **Quick test** – open the TileJSON URL in a browser. You should see something like: ```json { "tiles": ["https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"], "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14, "vector_layers": [ {"id":"transportation","description":"…"}, {"id":"water","description":"…"}, {"id":"landuse","description":"…"} ] } ``` If `vector_layers` is present, copy the exact `id` values – those are the strings you must use for `source-layer` in your style layers. --- ## 2️⃣ Verify every style layer’s `source-layer` matches the TileJSON schema ```json { "id": "my-roads", "type": "line", "source": "my-tiles", "source-layer": "transportation", // <-- must be *exactly* as in TileJSON "paint": { "line-color": "#ff6600", "line-width": 2 } } ``` **Common pitfalls** | Symptom | Typical cause | |---------|----------------| | No error, but the layer never appears | `source-layer` typo, wrong case, or using a layer name from a different schema (e.g., “roads” instead of “transportation”). | | All custom layers are invisible, but the basemap (provider’s style) works | You added the source **after** the provider’s style layers, but you never referenced the same source ID. Make sure the `source` property points to the source you just added (`my-tiles`). | | You see the layer in the style editor but nothing on the map | The source is there, but the `source-layer` name is wrong. Use the TileJSON `vector_layers` list to double-check. | **How to inspect the schema quickly** ```js fetch('https://tiles.example.com/tileset.json') .then(r => r.json()) .then(t => console.log(t.vector_layers.map(l => l.id))); ``` Copy the printed array and paste the exact strings into your style. --- ## 3️⃣ Insert your layers **below** the first symbol (label) layer If you add a layer with `map.addLayer(myLayer)` **without a second argument**, it goes on top of everything – including street-name labels. That often looks like “my data hides the map”, but the map is still rendering; you just can’t see the labels. **Solution** ```js // Find the first symbol layer (usually a label layer) const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id; // Add your custom layer *before* that layer map.addLayer(myLayer, firstSymbolId); ``` If you have many custom layers, add them in the order you want, always using the same `firstSymbolId` as the insertion point. --- ## 4️⃣ Make sure the style’s root assets are present | Asset | What happens if missing | What to check | |-------|--------------------------|---------------| | `glyphs` | Text appears in the browser’s default font (GL JS ≥ 5.11) – you’ll notice the wrong typeface, not missing text. | Open the glyph URL in a browser (replace `{fontstack}` and `{range}` with real values, e.g. `Open+Sans/0-255.pbf`). | | `sprite` | All icons (including shield icons, markers, etc.) disappear silently. | Open `.json` and `.png` URLs directly – they should return a JSON file and a PNG. | | CORS headers | Browser blocks the request → network tab shows **blocked** and the map is blank. | Look at the Network tab → response header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. If missing, add it on the server or CDN. | If you’re using the provider’s style URL, those assets are already baked in. When you write your own style you must **copy** the `glyphs` and `sprite` entries from the provider’s style (or host your own). ```json { "glyphs": "https://tiles.example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "sprite": "https://tiles.example.com/sprites/basic" } ``` --- ## 5️⃣ Feature-state sanity check (optional, but often a hidden gotcha) If you plan to use `setFeatureState` (hover, click, etc.) and you see no visual change: 1. **Make sure the source’s features have an `id`.** - For GeoJSON sources you can set `promoteId: 'my_id_property'`. - For vector sources you can also use `promoteId` (object form if the id lives in a specific source-layer). 2. **Do not rely on `generateId: true`** unless you are okay with IDs changing on every `setData` call. ```js map.addSource('parcels', { type: 'vector', url: 'https://tiles.example.com/parcels.json', promoteId: { parcels: 'parcel_id' } // <-- property name inside the parcel source-layer }); ``` Now `map.setFeatureState({source: 'parcels', sourceLayer: 'parcels', id: '12345'}, {hover:true})` will work. --- ## 6️⃣ Full “blank-map” diagnostic flow | Symptom | First thing to look at | |---------|------------------------| | **Network shows 404/blocked** | CORS or wrong tile URL (check the TileJSON). | | **Network shows 200 but nothing draws** | `source-layer` mismatch – compare with TileJSON `vector_layers`. | | **Map draws but labels disappear** | Layer order – insert before first `symbol` layer. | | **Map draws but at the wrong zoom** | Hand-wired `tiles` source missing `minzoom`/`maxzoom` (or raster `tileSize` wrong). | | **Icons missing** | Missing or wrong `sprite` URL. | | **Text in wrong font** | `glyphs` URL failing or missing. | | **Hover/selection does nothing** | No `id` on features → add `promoteId`. | --- ## 7️⃣ Minimal reproducible example ```html Custom style against hosted tiles
``` Replace `https://tiles.example.com/...` with the URLs your provider gives you. If the map now shows the basemap **and** the orange roads, you’ve wired everything correctly. --- ## 8️⃣ Quick “cheat-sheet” for the most common failure | Problem | One-line fix | |---------|--------------| | Blank map, network 200s | Check `source-layer` names against TileJSON `vector_layers`. | | Custom data hides street names | Insert layer before the first `symbol` layer (`addLayer(layer, firstSymbolId)`). | | Tiles appear but are blurry / off-zoom | For raster tiles add `tileSize: 256` (or the correct size). | | No icons | Add the provider’s `sprite` URL to the style root. | | Text looks wrong | Add the provider’s `glyphs` URL (or host your own). | | Hover/selection never works | Add `promoteId` (or `id` field) to the source. | | Requests blocked in console | Enable CORS on the tile/glyph/sprite host. | --- ### TL;DR 1. **Add the source with `url` (TileJSON) or a fully-specified `tiles` array + zoom range.** 2. **Copy the exact `source-layer` names from the TileJSON’s `vector_layers`.** 3. **Insert your layers before the first symbol layer** so you don’t cover labels. 4. **Copy the provider’s `glyphs` and `sprite` URLs** (or host your own). 5. **If you need feature-state, set `promoteId`** so features have stable IDs. 6. **Make sure CORS headers are present** on every cross-origin request. Follow those steps and your custom style will render exactly as the provider’s style does—only with your own layers on top. Happy mapping!

Description: explicit — TileJSON url vs hand-wired tiles template
prompt: In a MapLibre vector source, should I use the `url` field pointing at a TileJSON endpoint, or just put the {z}/{x}/{y} template straight into the `tiles` array? My tile server offers both.
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:**  
If the server gives you a TileJSON endpoint, point the source’s **`url`** at it.  
Only fall back to a hand-written **`tiles`** array when a TileJSON document does **not** exist (or you need to override something the TileJSON doesn’t expose).

---

## Why `url` is usually the right choice

| What you get from a TileJSON (`url`) | What you have to supply yourself when you use `tiles` |
|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **Tile URL template** (the same `{z}/{x}/{y}` string) | You must write the template yourself |
| **Zoom range** (`minzoom`, `maxzoom`) | If you omit them MapLibre assumes `maxzoom: 22`. The client will request zoom levels the tileset doesn’t have, get empty tiles and you’ll see “tiles appear then vanish as you zoom”. |
| **Bounds** (`bounds`) | Optional, but useful for `fitBounds` and for the style’s `source`-level `maxzoom` calculations |
| **Attribution** (`attribution`) | You have to copy it manually |
| **`vector_layers` list** – the exact `source-layer` names and their fields | You have to look them up elsewhere (documentation, `tippecanoe`/`planetiler` config, etc.) |
| **Encoding hints** (`encoding`, `format`) | Must be guessed or hard-coded |
| **CORS & other HTTP headers** are already served for the TileJSON URL, and the same origin is used for the tile requests | No extra benefit, but you still need CORS on the tile host |

Because the TileJSON contains *all* of the above, using `url` eliminates a whole class of silent-failure bugs:

* **Missing `source-layer`** – you can read the authoritative list from `vector_layers` and be sure you’re spelling it correctly.
* **Wrong zoom range** – the client will never request tiles that don’t exist.
* **Incorrect attribution** – you stay compliant with the tile provider’s licensing.
* **Future-proofing** – if the provider adds new layers or changes the zoom range, the TileJSON will reflect that automatically; you don’t have to edit your style.

---

## When you *must* use `tiles`

| Situation | Reason |
|-----------|--------|
| The provider only gives a raw URL template (e.g. `https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.png`) and no TileJSON endpoint. | There’s nothing to point `url` at. |
| You need to **override** a value that the TileJSON supplies (e.g. force `tileSize: 256` on a raster source that reports 512). | You can still use `url` **and** add the overriding fields, but if the provider doesn’t expose the field you need, you have to hand-wire the source. |
| You are building a **static style bundle** that must be completely self-contained (no extra network request for a TileJSON). | Embedding the template avoids an extra HTTP round-trip, but you lose the automatic metadata. |
| You are experimenting in a REPL or CodePen and want the shortest possible source definition. | A one-liner with `tiles` works, but be aware of the missing metadata. |

Even in those cases you should **manually add** the missing metadata (`minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `attribution`, `promoteId` if needed, etc.) to avoid the silent-failure pitfalls described above.

---

## Quick checklist before you decide

1. **Is there a TileJSON URL?**  
   - `https://example.com/tiles.json` → **use `url`.**  
   - No TileJSON → you must use `tiles`.

2. **Do you need any custom overrides?**  
   - If you need to change something the TileJSON already provides (e.g., `tileSize`), you can still use `url` **and** add the override field in the same source object.  
   - If the provider’s TileJSON is missing a field you need, you’ll have to hand-wire `tiles` and supply the missing fields yourself.

3. **Do you want automatic `source-layer` discovery?**  
   - `url` → `vector_layers` list is available in the TileJSON, making it easy to copy the exact names.  
   - `tiles` → you must look up the schema elsewhere (documentation, `tippecanoe` config, etc.).

4. **Are you concerned about CORS?**  
   - Both approaches need the tile host to send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.  
   - Using `url` adds one extra request (the TileJSON) but that request is also subject to CORS, so the same server must be configured either way.

5. **Performance / bundle size?**  
   - The extra TileJSON request is tiny (a few hundred bytes) and cached by the browser. The benefit of correct metadata almost always outweighs the cost.

---

## Example – preferred way (TileJSON)

```json
{
  "id": "basemap",
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "https://tiles.example.com/tileset.json"
}
```

*MapLibre will fetch `tileset.json`, read the `tiles` template, `minzoom`/`maxzoom`, `vector_layers`, etc., and you can immediately reference the correct `source-layer` names in your style layers.*

---

## Example – fallback (no TileJSON)

```json
{
  "id": "basemap",
  "type": "vector",
  "tiles": ["https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "attribution": "© Example Tiles",
  "bounds": [-180, -85, 180, 85]
}
```

*Make sure you **add** `minzoom`/`maxzoom` (otherwise MapLibre will request up to 22), and double-check the `source-layer` names against the provider’s documentation.*

---

## TL;DR

| Condition | Recommended field |
|-----------|-------------------|
| TileJSON endpoint exists | **`url`** (let MapLibre read the metadata) |
| No TileJSON, only a raw template | **`tiles`** (and manually add missing metadata) |
| Need to override a TileJSON value | Use **`url`** *plus* the overriding property in the same source object |
| Want the absolute minimal source definition for a quick demo | `tiles` works, but remember to add `minzoom`/`maxzoom` to avoid “tiles disappear at higher zooms”. |

Following this rule eliminates the most common “nothing renders, no error” failures (missing `source-layer`, wrong zoom range, missing attribution) and gives you a more robust, future-proof style. Happy mapping!

Description: implicit — literal {z}/{x}/{y} template fetched directly is not a server outage
prompt: My vector source uses tiles: ['https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf']. I pasted that exact URL into my browser address bar to check it works, and got an HTTP 500 error. Does this mean the tile server is down or broken?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
No – an HTTP 500 you see when you paste the literal template **`https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`** into a browser does **not** prove that the tile service is down. The server is receiving the literal string “{z}/{x}/{y}” instead of real numeric zoom, column and row values, and most tile servers will treat that as a malformed request and return a 500 (or 400/404) error.

### Why the 500 happens

| What you typed | What the server receives | Typical server reaction |
|----------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| `https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` | `…/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` (the braces are **not** replaced) | “Bad request / internal error” → 500 (or 400/404) |

MapLibre (and any other slippy-map client) replaces the three tokens **`{z}`**, **`{x}`**, **`{y}`** with numbers **before** it makes the HTTP request. A browser does not do that replacement, so you are asking the server for a tile that literally contains the characters `{`, `z`, `}` etc. Most tile servers are not programmed to handle that path and answer with a generic server-error response.

### How to verify the endpoint really works

1. **Pick a real tile coordinate** that you know is inside the source’s zoom range.  
   The simplest is the “world-cover” tile at zoom 0:

   ```
   https://tiles.example.com/0/0/0.pbf
   ```

   If the source’s `minzoom` is > 0, pick the next zoom level that exists, e.g. `1/0/0.pbf` or `2/1/1.pbf`.

2. **Open that concrete URL** in the browser (or curl/wget).  
   - **200 OK** and a binary response (you’ll see “garbled” text) → the server is serving tiles correctly.  
   - **404 Not Found** → the tile you asked for does not exist (maybe you’re outside the bounds or the zoom is too high/low).  
   - **500 Internal Server Error** → the server is genuinely failing for that tile; you’ll need to look at server logs or contact the provider.

3. **Check the network tab** while the map is loading.  
   - Look for requests to `…/0/0/0.pbf`, `…/1/0/0.pbf`, etc.  
   - Verify the status codes, response sizes, and **CORS** headers (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`).  
   - If you see **200** but the map is still blank, the problem is elsewhere (source-layer mismatch, missing `source-layer`, etc.).

### Quick diagnostic checklist for a vector source that uses `tiles`

| Symptom | First thing to verify |
|---------|-----------------------|
| **Blank map, network shows 500** | Did you request the literal template? Try a concrete tile (`/0/0/0.pbf`). |
| **Blank map, network shows 200 but nothing draws** | Check `source-layer` names against the TileJSON’s `vector_layers` (or the provider’s schema). |
| **Blank map, network shows 200, correct `source-layer`** | Verify the style’s `source-layer` is spelled exactly, and that the layer’s `type` (line, fill, symbol, …) matches the data. |
| **Labels/icons missing** | Ensure `glyphs` and `sprite` URLs are correct and CORS-enabled. |
| **Zoom-level appears off** | For raster sources, confirm `tileSize: 256` if the server serves 256-px tiles. For vector sources, missing `minzoom`/`maxzoom` on a hand-wired `tiles` array can cause the client to request zooms the tileset doesn’t have. |

### Example of a correctly-wired vector source

```json
{
  "id": "my-basemap",
  "type": "vector",
  "tiles": ["https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "attribution": "© Example Tiles"
}
```

If the provider also publishes a TileJSON endpoint (e.g. `https://tiles.example.com/tiles.json`), **prefer `url`**:

```json
{
  "id": "my-basemap",
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "https://tiles.example.com/tiles.json"
}
```

Using `url` lets MapLibre read the official `vector_layers` list, zoom range, bounds, and any other metadata automatically, reducing the chance of the above wiring errors.

### TL;DR steps to prove the server is alive

1. Replace the template with real numbers: `https://tiles.example.com/0/0/0.pbf`.
2. If you get **200**, the server is fine; the 500 you saw was just the result of using the un-expanded template.
3. If you still get **500**, the server truly has an internal error for that tile – contact the tile-service maintainer or check server logs.

Once you have a working tile request, move on to the next wiring checks (source-layer names, layer order, CORS, glyphs/sprites, `promoteId` for feature state, etc.) as described in the **MapLibre Source Wiring** skill.

`tiles: ['https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png']` | **`tileSize: 256`** | The default raster `tileSize` in MapLibre is **512 px**. // 3️⃣ Add the raster layer *below* that symbol layer map.addLayer( { id: 'osm-basemap', type: 'raster', source: 'osm-basemap', paint: { // optional: control opacity, contrast, etc. // 'raster-opacity': 1 } }, firstSymbolId // ← insert before the first symbol layer ); ``` ### What each line does | Line | Explanation | |------|-------------| | `type: 'raster'` | Tells MapLibre the tiles are raster images (PNG in this case). | | `tiles: [...]` | URL template with `{z}/{x}/{y}` placeholders. | | `tileSize: 256` | Matches OSM’s 256 px tiles; without it the map would be rendered at the wrong zoom level. | | `attribution` | Fulfills OSM’s usage policy and also shows up in the default `MapLibre` attribution control. | | `minzoom` / `maxzoom` | Limits requests to the zoom levels OSM actually provides (0-19). | | `firstSymbolId` | Dynamically discovers the first label layer so the basemap never hides street names, regardless of which style you start from. | | `addLayer(..., firstSymbolId)` | Inserts the raster layer **below** that symbol layer, preserving labels and icons. | --- ## Common pitfalls you’ll now avoid | Symptom | What you probably missed | Fix | |---------|--------------------------|-----| | **Basemap looks blurry / “zoomed out”** | No `tileSize: 256` (default 512) | Add `tileSize: 256`. | | **Map is completely blank** | Source added but no layer referencing it | Add a `raster` layer (`addLayer`). | | **Street names disappear** | Raster layer added after all symbol layers | Insert raster layer before the first `symbol` layer (see code above). | | **CORS error in console** | Using a custom tile server without CORS headers | Ensure the server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` (OSM already does). | | **Missing “© OpenStreetMap” text** | No attribution supplied | Add `attribution` to the source or display it yourself. | --- ## Quick sanity-check checklist before you run 1. **Source definition** includes `tileSize: 256`. 2. **Layer definition** exists, points to the source, and is added **before** the first `symbol` layer (or at the very bottom of the style). 3. **Network tab** shows successful `200` responses for tile URLs (e.g., `https://tile.openstreetmap.org/5/10/12.png`). 4. **Console** shows no CORS or 404 errors. 5. **Attribution** appears (or you’ve added it elsewhere). If all of the above are true, the OSM raster tiles will render at the correct scale, with labels on top, and you’ll be compliant with OSM’s usage policy. Happy mapping!

Description: anti-pattern — a glyph URL is not a vector tile source (the .pbf collision)
prompt: My style's glyphs property points to https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf. Since it's already working and ends in .pbf, can I also register that same URL as a vector tile source, or do I need a separate one for tiles?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:**  
No – the URL you give to the `glyphs` property is **only** a glyph-PBF endpoint. It cannot be used as a vector-tile source, and you must supply a **different** URL (or `tiles` array) that points to actual vector-tile PBFs.

Below is a quick why-this-doesn’t-work, followed by the exact steps you need to add a proper vector-tile source to the same style.

---

## 1. Glyph-PBFs ≠ Vector-Tile PBFs

|                     | Glyph PBF (`{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`) | Vector Tile PBF (`{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`) |
|---------------------|---------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| **What it contains** | Pre-rasterised outlines of a single font face for a specific Unicode range (e.g., 0-255, 256-511). No layer names, no feature properties. | One or more *layers* (e.g., `road`, `water`) each with many *features* (points, lines, polygons) and their attribute tables. |
| **Spec**            | **Mapbox Glyphs spec** – a tiny binary format that the style engine reads only when it needs to draw text. | **Mapbox Vector Tile spec** – a protobuf that the GPU can decode into geometry for rendering. |
| **URL tokens**      | `{fontstack}` and `{range}` – the style engine substitutes the requested font name and Unicode range. | `{z}`, `{x}`, `{y}` – the tile coordinates. |
| **How MapLibre treats it** | Loaded by the **style root** (`glyphs`), cached globally, never appears as a source. | Loaded as a **source** (`type: "vector"` or `"raster"`), appears in `map.getSource()`, can be queried with `queryRenderedFeatures`, etc. |
| **Can you register it as a source?** | **No** – MapLibre will try to fetch a tile like `0/0/0.pbf` from that URL, which will return a glyph PBF (or 404) and the source will never render anything. | **Yes** – but only if the endpoint actually serves vector tiles. |

Because the two formats are completely different, MapLibre will not magically reinterpret a glyph PBF as a vector tile. The request pattern, the protobuf schema, and the way the data is consumed are unrelated.

---

## 2. What you actually need for a vector-tile source

### 2.1 Choose the right endpoint type

| Situation | Recommended source definition |
|-----------|-------------------------------|
| **TileJSON endpoint** (e.g., `https://example.com/tileset.json`) | ```json { "type": "vector", "url": "https://example.com/tileset.json" } ``` |
| **Raw URL template** (no TileJSON) | ```json { "type": "vector", "tiles": ["https://example.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"], "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14 } ``` |
| **PMTiles** (or other custom protocol) | Register the protocol first (`pmtiles.addProtocol()`), then use `url: "pmtiles://mytiles.pmtiles"` |

> **Tip:** Even if you host the glyphs and the vector tiles on the same domain, keep the paths separate, e.g.  
> `https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` (glyphs)  
> `https://example.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` (vector tiles)

### 2.2 Minimal required fields for a vector source

```js
map.addSource('my-basemap', {
  type: 'vector',
  // either url or tiles, not both
  url: 'https://example.com/tileset.json',   // <-- preferred if you have TileJSON
  // tiles: ['https://example.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf'],
  // minzoom: 0,
  // maxzoom: 14,
  // attribution: '© Example Corp.'
});
```

*If you *must* use a hand-wired `tiles` array, **always** provide `minzoom`/`maxzoom`. Otherwise MapLibre assumes `maxzoom: 22` and will request zoom levels that don’t exist, which results in empty tiles.*

### 2.3 Wire the source into a layer

```js
map.addLayer({
  id: 'roads',
  type: 'line',
  source: 'my-basemap',
  'source-layer': 'transportation',   // <-- must match a layer name in the TileJSON
  paint: { 'line-color': '#ff6600', 'line-width': 2 }
});
```

If you get no error but nothing draws, the first thing to check is that `'source-layer'` exactly matches a name listed in the TileJSON’s `vector_layers` array.

---

## 3. Common pitfalls that look like “glyphs vs tiles” confusion

| Symptom | Likely cause (often mistaken for glyph-vs-tile) |
|---------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Blank map, network shows **200** for glyph requests but **404** for tile requests | Wrong `tiles` URL or missing `{z}/{x}/{y}` tokens. |
| Map shows geometry but **no text** | `glyphs` URL is wrong, CORS blocked, or the glyph endpoint returns 404/403. |
| Text appears but in a **system font** | Glyphs URL is unreachable; MapLibre falls back to the browser’s default font (since v5.11). |
| Geometry appears at the **wrong scale** | Raster source `tileSize` mismatch (256 vs 512) – not a glyph issue. |
| `setFeatureState` does nothing | Source features lack an `id` (use `promoteId`). |

---

## 4. Quick checklist for your current setup

1. **Glyphs** – keep `glyphs: "https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf"` in the style root.  
   *Make sure the server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` and the correct `Content-Type: application/x-protobuf`.*

2. **Vector tiles** – add a **separate** source definition, e.g.:

   ```js
   map.addSource('my-tiles', {
     type: 'vector',
     url: 'https://example.com/tileset.json'   // or tiles: [...]
   });
   ```

3. **Layers** – reference that source with the proper `source-layer` name.

4. **CORS** – both the glyph endpoint **and** the tile endpoint must allow cross-origin requests. If you host them on the same domain you can usually skip extra config, but if they are on different subdomains or a CDN, add the appropriate CORS headers.

5. **Test** – open the Network tab, request a concrete tile, e.g. `https://example.com/tiles/0/0/0.pbf`. You should get a **vector-tile** protobuf (size ~10-30 KB). Request a glyph range, e.g. `https://example.com/fonts/Open+Sans/0-255.pbf`; you’ll see a much smaller file (~2-5 KB). If the two look the same (both 200 KB, same content), you’re probably hitting the wrong endpoint.

---

## 5. TL;DR for your exact question

- **No**, you cannot register the glyphs URL (`https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`) as a vector-tile source.  
- **Yes**, you need a **different** URL (or TileJSON) that serves true vector tiles (`{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`).  
- You can host both under the same domain, but they must be distinct paths and follow their own spec.

If you already have a TileJSON for the same dataset, just point `url` at that. If you only have raw tile URLs, use the `tiles` array and remember to set `minzoom`/`maxzoom`. Once that source is added, create layers that reference it, and your glyphs will continue to work unchanged.

---

### Further reading

- **MapLibre Style Spec – `glyphs`**: <https://maplibre.org/maplibre-style-spec/#glyphs>
- **MapLibre Style Spec – Vector source**: <https://maplibre.org/maplibre-style-spec/sources/#vector>
- **TileJSON `vector_layers`**: <https://github.com/mapbox/tilejson-spec/tree/master/3.0.0#vector_layers>

Feel free to paste your current source definition if you’d like a concrete review!

Description: implicit — a mapbox:// URL is not directly usable in MapLibre
prompt: A colleague sent me mapbox://styles/mapbox/streets-v11 for us to use as a vector source in our MapLibre map. Can we just drop that URL into a vector source's `url` field?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:** No. The `mapbox://styles/...` URL is a *style* URL, not a TileJSON (or tile-template) that a MapLibre **source** can consume. Drop-in it will not work – MapLibre will try to treat it as a TileJSON endpoint, get back a style document, and then silently render nothing.

Below is a quick-reference checklist that explains why, what you can actually use, and the steps to get a working vector source from a Mapbox-hosted tileset.

---

## 1️⃣ What the `mapbox://styles/...` URL really is

| URL | What you get when you fetch it | What MapLibre expects for a **vector source** |
|-----|-------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `mapbox://styles/mapbox/streets-v11` | **Style JSON** (the whole map style – layers, sources, glyphs, sprites, etc.) | **TileJSON** (metadata + `tiles` array) **or** a plain tile-template (`{z}/{x}/{y}`) |
| `mapbox://tileset/...` (e.g. `mapbox://tileset/username/tileset-id`) | **TileJSON** (if you request the `.json` endpoint) or a tile-template when you add `/{z}/{x}/{y}` | ✅ What a source’s `url` field wants |

A style JSON contains *source definitions* inside it, but it is **not** the source definition itself. MapLibre can load a style JSON via `map.setStyle(styleUrl)` (or `new maplibregl.Map({style: styleUrl})`), but you cannot point a source’s `url` at a style URL.

---

## 2️⃣ How MapLibre expects a vector source to be defined

```json
{
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "https://example.com/tileset.json"          // TileJSON endpoint
}
```

or, when you prefer to write the template yourself:

```json
{
  "type": "vector",
  "tiles": [
    "https://example.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"
  ],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14
}
```

The **only** thing that can go in the `url` field is a URL that returns a **TileJSON** document (or a `pmtiles://` URL that the PMTiles plugin knows how to read). The TileJSON must contain a `tiles` array, `vector_layers` metadata, and (optionally) `minzoom`/`maxzoom`.

---

## 3️⃣ Getting a TileJSON for a Mapbox tileset

If you have a Mapbox **tileset** (e.g. the built-in `mapbox.mapbox-streets-v8` that backs `streets-v11`), you can request its TileJSON directly from the Mapbox Tiles API:

```
https://api.mapbox.com/v4/mapbox.mapbox-streets-v8.json?access_token=YOUR_MAPBOX_TOKEN
```

*or* the newer Tileset API (v4 → v5) format:

```
https://api.mapbox.com/v4/mapbox.mapbox-streets-v8.json?access_token=YOUR_MAPBOX_TOKEN
```

Both return a TileJSON document that looks like:

```json
{
  "tiles": [
    "https://api.mapbox.com/v4/mapbox.mapbox-streets-v8/{z}/{x}/{y}.vector.pbf?access_token=YOUR_MAPBOX_TOKEN"
  ],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "vector_layers": [
    { "id": "road", "fields": { "class": "String", "name": "String" }, "minzoom": 5, "maxzoom": 14 },
    …
  ]
}
```

That URL **can** be used as the source’s `url`:

```js
map.addSource('mb-streets', {
  type: 'vector',
  url: 'https://api.mapbox.com/v4/mapbox.mapbox-streets-v8.json?access_token=pk.ey...'
});
```

> **Important:** The request must include a **valid Mapbox access token** (`pk.ey...` for public tokens, `sk.ey...` for secret ones). If you omit the token, the request will 401 and the map will stay blank.

---

## 4️⃣ Alternative: Use the style directly (if you just want the whole Mapbox Streets map)

If you really want the *entire* Mapbox Streets style (including its own layers, glyphs, sprites, etc.) you can load it as a **style**, not as a source:

```js
new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: 'https://api.mapbox.com/styles/v1/mapbox/streets-v11?access_token=YOUR_MAPBOX_TOKEN',
  center: [0, 0],
  zoom: 2
});
```

MapLibre will treat the URL as a style JSON, fetch the embedded sources (which are TileJSON URLs like the one above), and render the map exactly like Mapbox GL JS would—*provided* you have a token and the Mapbox CDN is reachable.

> **Caveat:** This works only if you are okay with using Mapbox-hosted assets (glyphs, sprites, tiles) and you respect Mapbox’s licensing. If you need a *custom* style that mixes your own sources with Mapbox’s basemap, you’ll still need the TileJSON approach for the Mapbox source.

---

## 5️⃣ Common pitfalls that look like “just drop the URL”

| Symptom | Why it happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| Map stays blank, network shows a GET to `https://api.mapbox.com/styles/v1/mapbox/streets-v11?...` with 200, but no tiles load | You passed a **style URL** to a source; MapLibre expects TileJSON, so it never finds any `tiles` array. | Use the TileJSON endpoint (`.../v4/mapbox.mapbox-streets-v8.json?...`) or load the style as a whole. |
| CORS errors in the console | The request to `api.mapbox.com` lacks the `access_token` query param, or the token is for a *restricted* domain. | Append a valid public token (`pk.ey...`) to the URL, or configure `transformRequest` to inject the token automatically. |
| Tiles appear but are all gray/blank | You used the TileJSON but omitted the token in the `tiles` URLs (Mapbox returns 401 for each tile). | Ensure the token is present in the TileJSON (Mapbox includes it automatically) **or** add it via `transformRequest`. |
| `source-layer` errors (nothing draws) | You added a layer with `source-layer: "road"` but the TileJSON’s `vector_layers` list uses `road` **or** `road` is not present in that tileset. | Inspect the TileJSON’s `vector_layers` array (or use the Mapbox Style editor) to get the exact layer names (`road`, `road_label`, etc.). |
| `setFeatureState` does nothing | The source has no feature IDs because you didn’t set `promoteId`. | For a Mapbox vector source you can’t set `promoteId` (IDs are already baked in). Use the built-in IDs or a separate GeoJSON source for interactive features. |

---

## 6️⃣ Quick “copy-paste” recipe

```js
// 1️⃣ Add the Mapbox Streets vector source (TileJSON)
map.addSource('mb-streets', {
  type: 'vector',
  url: 'https://api.mapbox.com/v4/mapbox.mapbox-streets-v8.json?access_token=pk.eyYOUR_PUBLIC_TOKEN'
});

// 2️⃣ Add a layer that uses it (example: water polygons)
map.addLayer({
  id: 'water',
  type: 'fill',
  source: 'mb-streets',
  'source-layer': 'water',          // exact name from TileJSON.vector_layers
  paint: {
    'fill-color': '#a0c8f0',
    'fill-opacity': 0.6
  }
});
```

If you need the **full Mapbox Streets style** (including labels, icons, etc.) and you just want to overlay a few of your own layers, the simplest approach is:

```js
const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: 'https://api.mapbox.com/styles/v1/mapbox/streets-v11?access_token=pk.eyYOUR_PUBLIC_TOKEN',
  center: [-122.447303, 37.753574],
  zoom: 12
});

// When the style is loaded, add your custom source/layer(s)
map.on('style.load', () => {
  map.addSource('my-data', { type: 'geojson', data: myGeojson });
  map.addLayer({
    id: 'my-points',
    type: 'circle',
    source: 'my-data',
    paint: { 'circle-radius': 6, 'circle-color': '#ff6600' }
  });
});
```

---

## 7️⃣ TL;DR Checklist

- **Never** put `mapbox://styles/...` into a source’s `url`.  
- Use a **TileJSON** endpoint (`…/v4/<tileset>.json?...`) or a `tiles` template that includes a valid Mapbox token.  
- If you just want the whole Mapbox style, load it as a **style**, not as a source.  
- Remember CORS & token: Mapbox requires `access_token` on every request; MapLibre will forward it automatically only if it’s part of the URL or you add it via `transformRequest`.  
- Verify the `source-layer` names against the TileJSON’s `vector_layers` array.  

Once you switch from the style URL to a proper TileJSON (or load the style directly), the vector source will render as expected. Happy mapping!
